h1: Cellar temperature and humidity for ageing beer at home
title: Cellar Temperature and Humidity for Beer | Craft Beer School
desc: The right temperature and humidity for ageing beer at home, why stability matters more than the exact number and when humidity counts.
teaser: Twelve degrees, steady and dark. Humidity matters less than people think, unless there is a cork.
standfirst: Ageing beer at home comes down to a few conditions: temperature, stability, darkness and, for corked bottles, humidity. Here is what each one does and the numbers to aim for.
sections:
Most brewers and cellar guides agree on about 10 to 13 °C (50 to 55 °F) as the range for ageing strong beer. In that window, the slow changes you want happen at a reasonable pace: harsh alcohol softens, sharp roast rounds off, dried fruit and sherry-like notes develop.

Some people prefer slightly warmer, up to around 15 °C, for big beers they want to mature faster. Others use colder storage, which slows everything. There is no single correct figure, only a trade-off between speed and control.

Most of the changes in a stored beer are chemical reactions, especially slow oxidation. As a rough rule of thumb, reaction rates roughly double or triple with every 10 °C rise. Beer kept at 30 °C, common in Indian homes in summer, ages several times faster than beer at 12 °C.

Fast ageing is not better ageing. At high temperatures stale flavours such as cardboard, honey and toffee appear quickly, as our guide to ageing notes in pale beer explains. The pleasant changes of slow cellaring often never get the chance.
Stability matters more than the exact number

A beer stored at a steady 15 °C will usually age better than one that swings between 8 °C at night and 25 °C in the day. Temperature swings make the liquid and the headspace gas expand and contract, which can draw tiny amounts of air past a cap or cork. They also produce uneven ageing.

Aim for daily variation of no more than a couple of degrees. A thermostatically controlled wine or beverage cooler does this easily. Our guide to setting a home beer fridge covers the controls.

Humidity matters mainly for corked bottles. A natural cork that dries out can shrink and let air in. Traditional wine cellars sit at around 60 to 70% relative humidity for this reason.

Most beer is sealed with a crown cap, which does not care about humidity at all. If your cellar is all crown-capped bottles, you can ignore humidity entirely. If you keep corked Belgian ales or lambics for several years, humidity in the 50 to 70% range helps. Very high humidity, above about 80%, brings its own problems: mould on labels and corks.

In much of India the air is humid enough for most of the year, especially in coastal cities. In a dry climate or an air-conditioned room, a small dish of water in the cooler can raise humidity a little.

Light, especially blue and ultraviolet, breaks down hop compounds and produces a skunky aroma. Brown glass blocks most of the harmful light. Clear and green glass block very little. In a cellar, keep everything dark: a solid door, an opaque box or a cupboard.

Also keep beer away from strong smells such as paint, onions or cleaning products, which can affect corks over time.

A cheap digital min-max thermometer or a small temperature logger is the most useful cellar tool you can buy. It shows not just the current temperature but the highest and lowest since you last reset it. Check it every week for the first month. You may find your 'cool' cupboard reaches 29 °C every afternoon.

Write the readings in your cellar records. Our guide to keeping a cellar log shows a simple format. Over time you will see whether the conditions you set are the ones your bottles actually get.
What warm storage does to the flavour

It helps to know what you are protecting against. In a strong dark beer stored too warm, the first signs are usually a papery or cardboard note in the aroma and a flattening of the malt. Rich chocolate and dark fruit give way to a dull, slightly sweet sherry character. Hop bitterness also fades steadily with age at any temperature, but heat speeds it up.

At cellar temperature these changes are slower and often pleasant in moderation. A barley wine that tastes hot and sharp when fresh may soften and pick up toffee and dried fruit notes over a year or two at 12 °C. The same beer kept at 30 °C may taste flat and stale within a few months.

Paler, hoppy beers never really benefit from warmth or time. If you buy an IPA, keep it in the fridge at 3 to 5 °C and drink it within a few weeks of the packaging date.

Numbers only tell you about conditions. Tasting tells you about results. Keep at least two bottles of each beer: one to open early as a reference and one to age. Taste them side by side when you open the aged one, if you saved a fresh one in the fridge.

Your first step: put a min-max thermometer where you plan to keep beer and leave it there for a week before buying any bottles to age. Let the thermometer tell you if the spot is good enough.
faqs: What temperature should I age beer at?
About 10 to 13 °C is the usual target for ageing strong beer. Stable temperature matters more than hitting an exact figure.
Only for corked bottles. Crown caps are unaffected. For corks, around 50 to 70% relative humidity helps.
Can I age beer at room temperature in India?
Briefly, but warm temperatures speed up staling. Summer room temperatures of 30 °C or more age beer far faster than a cellar.
Yes. Light can produce a skunky aroma quickly, especially in clear or green glass. Store beer in the dark.
